extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative principles for evaluating inductive arguments, axioms, hypotheses, and the use of syllogistic form in scientific and everyday reasoning. Focuses on when formal premises are mere aids, how axioms derive from experience, and how hypotheses and multiple theories should be interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: General and particular assertions proven by same evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the general proposition (e.g., 'All men are mortal') and the subsequent particular assertion concerning a new individual (e.g., Socrates is mortal) are proved together by the same grounds of experience on which the general assertion was made. The particular is not proved by the major alone but interpreted by the evidence that justified the generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the minor premise as proving the particular by virtue of the major alone. The evidence justifying the generalization is also the evidence for the particular; demonstrations that posit the major as antecedently including the conclusion mistake the epistemic order. Avoid circular reasoning that would require asserting, as a premise, what is later used to prove part of that premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the minor premise as interpretive identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal syllogistic minor (predicating of Socrates a class-name) is not logically necessary but serves to identify the precise kind of likeness the unobserved case bears to observed instances (e.g., 'Socrates is like A, B, C...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the minor as a precaution against error: it shows that the new individual possesses the marks specified by the major. In practice, when revising a rough inference from particulars, select two clear syllogistic premises to express the same evidence more transparently; use the minor to specify the kind of similarity required by the major.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism as representation, not necessary condition of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal major and minor premises are conveniences for expressing and checking an inference; reasoning can be and often is carried on without the syllogistic form in thought. Syllogistic premises 'start into existence together' as a corrective or record, not as preconditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syllogistic form when you need to revise, record, or judge an inference; do not conflate the existence of syllogistic premises with the existence of the underlying evidential support. Beware of assuming that adding formal premises adds evidence rather than merely clarifying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses in geometry as known fictions with certain true parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hypotheses (particularly in geometry) are known not to be literally true; nevertheless, those parts of them that are true are not hypothetical but certain. The hypothetical element makes the truth of conclusions conditional rather than categorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating geometric (or idealized) arguments, recognize that ideal assumptions are fictions approximating reality; conclusions are conditional on the idealization. Treat such hypotheses as methodological devices whose applicable portions supply certainty for derived results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms derived from experience and proved by approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical and mechanical axioms (e.g., 'Two straight lines cannot inclose a space') arise from observation and are justifiable by inductive methods such as proof by approximation and the Method of Concomitant Variations; mathematical limits exemplify the extreme case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand literal empirical instances of ideal concepts; instead, assess whether observed gradations approach the ideal so that the limiting inference is warranted. Evaluate axioms by their continual suggestion and verification across experience, and by whether approximation supports the limit-case claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of mental imagery varies by domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental recollections and imagery can serve as subjects of experimentation; geometrical forms are typically reproduced with higher precision in the mind than sensations such as colors or odors, so inferences from mental images are more trustworthy in geometry than in many other domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on recollection or imagination as evidence, assess domain-specific reliability and individual variation. Use mental imagery confidently for simple geometrical reasoning, but be cautious for domains (e.g., color, smell) where recollection is less precise and more variable between individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the 'inconceivability of the negative' as a test
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Universal Postulate' or test that rests on the inconceivability of a proposition's negation can be fallible in some cases; however, any such risk is incurred at early steps and is not automatically multiplied by the length of subsequent reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat inconceivability as an infallible proof technique. Distinguish between risks from the underlying postulate and risks from careless or ambiguous reasoning. Pay attention to sources of error like ambiguous terms, which can mislead whole communities or ages, rather than assuming longer argumentative chains are inherently less valid due to repetition of the postulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental 'mark' principle as basis for inductive inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning depends on the axiom that 'whatever has a mark, has what it is a mark of'—i.e., signs or marks observed in instances indicate the possession of the relevant property—and this axiom, repeated in thought, is the basis for drawing inferences from observed to unobserved cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inductive inferences by whether the marks identified are genuinely indicative of the claimed property. Consider whether the axiom (that marks imply property) is secure in the domain at hand; distinguish between the epistemic trustworthiness of the axiom itself and incidental reasoning errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad conception of induction including informal practical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction should not be confined to conscious generalization as in science; many practical inferences from particulars to particulars, made without explicit general propositions, are intellectually substantial and are essentially the same operation as scientific induction, differing mainly in the absence of explicit recording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing informal practical reasoning, acknowledge its legitimacy and potential intellectual equivalence to formal scientific induction. For scientific purposes require explicit general propositions (for record and critique), but do not dismiss everyday inductive inferences as non-inductive or inferior simply because they lack formal articulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility and interpretation of multiple theories/explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different theories or explanations about the same phenomena may all be true and consistent with each other if each is worked out so as to agree with the facts; some hypotheses that appear opposed may be reconciled by reformulation, though hypotheses that assert distinct material agents may be mutually exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating competing theories, distinguish between (a) explanatory descriptions or representational devices (which may be reconcilable) and (b) hypotheses that assert specific material mechanisms (which may be incompatible). Check whether apparent contradictions are terminological or substantive, and assess whether theories can be reconciled by showing they yield the same factual consequences.
